BOOK_B.title: Court-ordered costs award

commentary.text: Rule 10.31 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. Overview In V.L.M. v. Dominey Estate, 2023 ABCA 382, a class action lawsuit, the Court gave this very helpful explanation of the law of costs, and the factors to be considered: [4] The primary purpose of a costs award is to partly indemnify the successful party for the legal expenses it incurred in the proceedings. Costs awards may serve other purposes such as discouraging unnecessary steps in litigation, encouraging efficiency and proportionality in the steps that are taken, sanctioning bad or frivolous behavior, encouraging settlement, and promoting access to justice: British Columbia (Minister of Forests) v Okanagan Indian Band, 2003 SCC 71 at paras. 22-30, [2003] 3 SCR 371. [5] The Court has a wide discretion over what are “reasonable and proper costs … that the Court considers to be appropriate in the circumstances” under R. 10.31: McAllister v Calgary (City), 2021 ABCA 25 at paras. 25-26. A number of relevant factors are set out in R. 10.31 and 10.33. Costs are frequently awarded by reference to Schedule C, a method that has the advantage of providing the parties with greater certainty as to their exposure to costs, is simple, efficient, and inexpensive to apply, and in many cases avoids the need for lengthy inquiries into and assessment of the appropriate level of costs: McAllister at paras. 59-60, 62. The Court can, in appropriate cases, award costs without reference to Schedule C, for example by a lump sum costs award or by a percentage of solicitor and client costs. [6] Schedule C will in many cases represent an appropriate level of indemnification. The Schedule has as its basis an assumption about the relationship between the costs it would generate and solicitor and client costs that should have been incurred for similar pieces of litigation: Barkwell v McDonald (#1), 2023 ABCA 87 at para. 58. However, there is no presumption in the Rules that the successful party is entitled to any particular level of indemnification: McAllister at para. 31; Brosseau Estate v Dubarry Estate, 2023 ABKB 378 at para. 21. [7] McAllister is an example of litigation where the Court confirmed that after a lengthy trial a costs award based on a percentage of fees reasonably incurred might be appropriate. At an interlocutory stage the entitlement to some level of indemnification is less clear because overall success is unknown: McAllister at para. 64. For example, while certification is an important step in a class proceeding, there is no assurance that the class will ultimately be successful because certification does not engage an examination of the merits of the claim: Class Proceedings Act, SA 2003, c. C-16.5, s. 6(2). Quantum of the Costs Award [8] With respect to any costs award, particularly one based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees, the issue is not what counsel actually charged the successful litigant, but what costs should have been incurred in the litigation having regard to all of the relevant circumstances. The issue is not whether the fee charged to the client is fair to the client, but what amount the unsuccessful party can fairly be expected to contribute: Barkwell (#1) at paras. 57-59; Barkwell v McDonald (#2), 2023 ABCA 183 at paras. 74-75; Kantor v Kantor, 2023 ABCA 329 at paras. 12-13. [9] The overriding issue is proportionality. The rules on costs aim to balance indemnity of the winner without unreasonably discouraging access to the court, or unduly penalizing the losing party: McAllister at para. 45; Barkwell (#1) at para. 57. One of the dangers of a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees is that there is no clear disincentive to overly zealous, inefficient, or disproportionate litigation. In short, success is not a justification for disproportionate litigation. …. [13] Even where the Court exercises its discretion to make a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees actually charged, it is not sufficient for the successful party to simply assert entitlement to the total obtained by multiplying hours times hourly rate: Barkwell (#1) at para. 60. Some justification is required for all the components of the fees claim, such as the hourly rate, the number of hours worked, the number of counsel involved, and the proportionality of the litigation…. [14] Given the disadvantaged status of some of the class members, under R. 10.33(1)(g) access to justice is a relevant consideration in setting the costs award. However, the representative plaintiff has been able to retain counsel on a contingency fee basis, providing access to justice. The only issue being resolved at the moment is the costs of this appeal, not the costs of the overall class proceeding. Those costs will depend on the ultimate outcome of the class action. In Barkwell v. McDonald, 2023 ABCA 87, 2023 CarswellAlta 675, additional reasons 2023 ABCA 183, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 2751 (S.C.C.), the Court gave general guidance on the issue of costs: [53] As the decision in McAllister v Calgary (City), 2021 ABCA 25 confirms, trial judges have considerable discretion in setting “reasonable and proper costs” under R. 10.31(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010. The costs award need not be based on Schedule C in the Rules and indeed Schedule C is not a mandated default method: McAllister at para 54. However, as McAllister confirmed at para 58, that does not mean that Schedule C is without utility and “is used day in and day out by judges in a great variety of situations.” Using Schedule C has the advantage of providing parties with greater certainty as to their exposure to costs, it is simple, efficient, and inexpensive to apply, and in many cases avoids the need for lengthy inquiries into and assessment of the appropriate level of costs: McAllister at paras 59-60, 62. [54] Whenever the winning party seeks a lump sum costs award, that party should provide the court, as a benchmark, an assessment of the fees that would be ordered under Schedule C: McAllister at para 61. [55] McAllister confirms that the discretion of a trial judge over costs extends to awarding a percentage of the solicitor and client costs incurred by the successful party. That does not, however, mean that the winning party can simply assert the quantum of the fees that was charged by counsel, and paid by the winning party. As McAllister recognized by sending the costs award in that case back to the trial judge, a detailed analysis is required to determine “reasonable and proper costs”. [56] The starting point is to recognize the important distinction between solicitor and own client costs, and solicitor and client costs. Solicitor and own client costs are those costs that counsel can charge to the winning party, and that the winning party is required to pay as a matter of contract. Solicitor and client costs represent the costs that a reasonable client might be required to pay for the services rendered. It is rarely appropriate to award solicitor and own client costs as a costs award in litigation: Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 at paras 77-78, 53 Alta LR (6th) 44. [57] The overriding issue is proportionality. The rules on costs aim to balance indemnity of the winner without unreasonably discouraging access to the court, or unduly penalizing the losing party: McAllister at para 45. The winning party cannot simply claim a percentage of the fees paid if they are disproportionate to the issues and the amounts involved. Success is not a justification for disproportionate litigation. One important feature of the tariff in Schedule C is that it does not measure how much in fees was paid by the winning party, but rather, gives a rough measure of how much should have been incurred in the ordinary case having regard to the amounts in dispute. Obviously, the amount involved is not always determinative, but the principle of proportionality applies to non-monetary issues as well. [58] The long-established principle is that costs awards are designed to partially, but not fully indemnify the winning party: McAllister at para 37. It is frequently said that a rough rule of thumb is that the costs award should reflect 40 to 50% of the solicitor and client costs: McAllister at paras 41-42. That again is not necessarily a reference to the costs incurred and paid by the client, but rather to the costs that should reasonably have been incurred given the issues. This was also the benchmark that was used to set the tariff in Schedule C (McAllister at para 43), and why we stress that a party, regardless of the costs claimed, should always provide as a benchmark a draft Bill of Costs based on Schedule C. [59] Further, if the trial judge decides to make a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client costs the analysis must go further. The question is not just whether the solicitor and client costs are reasonable as between solicitor and client, but whether the quantum represents an amount that the losing party in the litigation should reasonably be expected to pay to the winning party. As confirmed in McAllister at paras 46, 48: If the option of awarding costs as a percentage of assessed costs is chosen, the assessment of the costs may require a consideration of what is a reasonable amount which ought to have been charged for the services the successful party’s lawyer rendered and that may require reference to the considerations set forth in Rule 10.2(1) which go into the determination of what constitutes a reasonable charge. . . That the lawyer’s charges are reasonable as between solicitor and client is not the end of the assessment. Consideration must also be given in assessing the reasonableness of requiring the unsuccessful party to indemnify the successful party for a percentage of them. [Emphasis added]. As McAllister notes, this involves a detailed analysis of all the factors that go into assessing solicitor’s fees: see R. 10.2 and R. 10.33. [60] If the winning party seeks a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees, that request must be justified by a consideration of the factors in R. 10.2 that are relevant to the reasonableness of a fee. That includes the importance of the issues, the circumstances of the client, the manner in which the services were provided, the skill and responsibility involved, and other relevant considerations. Many of those same issues are also listed in R. 10.33, which in addition to the amount in issue, refers to the complexity of the action and the conduct of the parties. Also relevant are things like the hourly rates being charged (including paralegal or administrative time), whether those rates were appropriate given the seniority and experience of counsel, whether the work was being done by lawyers of appropriate seniority, the number of counsel involved, whether the duration and intensity of pre-trial questioning was appropriate or excessive or disproportionate, whether unnecessary interlocutory proceedings were launched and the outcome of those proceedings, and whether the ultimate fee was proportionate to the issues. [61] In the costs decision under appeal the trial judge simply granted a costs award equal to 50% of the face value of the legal fees claimed by the respondent, without any further analysis and without a draft Bill of Costs based on Schedule C. That is not an approach sanctioned by McAllister. The above statements were quoted with approval in Sunridge Nissan Inc. v. McRuer, 2023 ABCA 128 at para. 57, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 3166 (S.C.C.). When the matter returned again to the Court of Appeal (Barkwell v. McDonald, 2023 ABCA 183, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 2751 (S.C.C.)), the Court reaffirmed its position on party and party costs based on solicitor client costs. The Court said: [74] As noted, the reasons on trial costs (2022 ABQB 208) awarded the respondent 50% of solicitor and client costs, relying on McAllister v Calgary (City), 2021 ABCA 25. As indicated in the appeal reasons, an award of party and party costs based on solicitor and client costs must be justified: 2023 ABCA 87 at paras. 52-61. The issue is not simply how much the successful party spent, but how much that party can reasonably expect the other party to pay. The amount actually charged to the client is not definitive. The rates and amount of time invested must be justified. The costs awarded must be proportionate to the amounts in issue. In McAllister v. Calgary (City), 2021 ABCA 25, 2021 CarswellAlta 152, 16 Alta. L.R. (7th) 291, the Court of Appeal addressed how a Court should calculate the appropriate costs to be awarded to a successful party. As the Court said (paragraph 4), “[t]his appeal involves a consideration of the level of indemnification a successful party to protracted litigation should receive in costs from the losing party, and in so doing it addresses the role of Schedule C in making such costs awards, as well as other types of costs awards.” It is respectfully submitted that the Court's statements provide valuable assistance in understanding how to properly implement the discretionary power granted by the Rules in relation to costs. [21] The Rules confer a qualified “entitlement” to costs to the successful party. Rule 10.29(1) states that a successful party is “entitled to a costs award against the unsuccessful party” and that the “unsuccessful party must pay the costs forthwith”. An award of costs is therefore the prima facie entitlement of the successful party, but that entitlement may not always obtain. … [23] In Alberta, the considerations which go into the determination of the amount of a costs award are set forth in Rule 10.33 …. [24] After the court has considered the factors described in Rule 10.33 with respect to quantum, the court is directed by the Rules to go to Rule 10.31 which provides options for making costs awards … [25] Thus, in making a costs award under 10.31(1)(a), as in this case, the court is provided with a menu of orders it may make with respect to costs. Rule 10.31(3)(a) expressly provides that “all or part of reasonable and proper costs” may be ordered, “with or without reference to Schedule C.” This suggests significant discretion on the part of a trial judge in implementing a reasonable and proper costs award and would appear to clearly permit an order for a lump sum percentage of legal costs. Rule 10.31(3)(d) expressly permits such a costs award. Rule 10.31(3)(b) permits the court to make an order directing the unsuccessful party to pay the successful party an amount equal to a multiple, a proportion or a fraction of an amount set out in any column of the Tariff of Recoverable Fees in Schedule C. [26] It is important to note that the options set forth in Rule 10.31(3) are expressly linked to Rule 10.31(1)(a), which permits the court to award “the reasonable and proper costs that a party incurred”. [27] What comes out of this analysis of the Rules is that a costs award made with reference to Schedule C is only one of several options open to a court in awarding costs to a successful party and that awarding a percentage of assessed costs is expressly authorized. [28] The trial judge attempted to apply “a principled approach which considers the purpose of costs”, but she appeared to perceive Schedule C to be the default rule, absent misconduct or complexity, for making cost awards. The Rules of Court do not support that characterization. Costs awards may or may not be based on Schedule C. A variety of means are countenanced by the Rules to arrive at a reasonable costs award (see Renke, J. in GO Community Centre v Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd, 2020 ABQB 203 at para 82). [29] To summarize, Schedule C is merely one of a number of options or tools that may be used to achieve the outcome of reasonable and proper costs under Rule 10.31(1)(a). Other options include not making any reference to Schedule C (Rule 10.31(3)(a)); or awarding costs pursuant to “a multiple, proportion or fraction of an amount set out in … Schedule C” (Rule 10.31(3)(b); or awarding a percentage of assessed costs (Rule 10.31(3)(d)). [30] A successful party is entitled either to reasonable and proper costs, as set out in Rule 10.31(1)(a), or to any other amount the court considers appropriate in the circumstances, as set out in Rule 10.31(1)(b). However, if the costs award is to be “the reasonable and proper costs that a party incurred” as provided for in Rule 10.31(1)(a), then the options with respect to making such costs award are set forth in Rule 10.31(3). B. — A Standard Level of Costs Indemnification [31] While Rules 10.31(1) and 10.33 lay out a framework for assessing costs and making cost awards, they provide little guidance as to what quantum of costs indemnification constitutes “reasonable and proper costs”. For example, the Rules do not specify a level of indemnification required to constitute reasonable and proper costs. … [33] A “reasonable and proper costs” award involves a payment by the unsuccessful party to the successful party to indemnify the successful party for expenses incurred as a result of the conduct of the unsuccessful party. The primary purpose of a costs award is to indemnify the successful party in respect of the expenses sustained either defending a claim that in the end proved unfounded (if the successful party was the defendant), or in pursuing a valid legal right (if the plaintiff prevailed) (Okanagan Indian Band at para 21). The indemnification is not intended to be complete. Nevertheless, a reasonable level of indemnification of costs incurred is the primary purpose of costs awards. Other considerations may come into play, but only when appropriate. For example, encouraging efficiency only comes into play where there is a specific opportunity to encourage it or where there has been a demonstrated inefficiency in the conduct of the litigation. [34] The Supreme Court in Okanagan Indian Band indicated that the traditional principles supporting costs awards continue to govern the law of costs in cases where there are no special factors that would warrant a departure from them (para 22). See also MM Orkin, The Law of Costs, 2nd ed (Aurora, ON: Canada Law Book, 2019) (loose-leaf updated 2020, release 89), ch 2 at 2–8, where the author indicates that indemnification is the “essence” of an award of party-and-party costs. Orkin cites Bell Canada v Consumers' Assoc of Canada, 1986 CanLII 49 (SCC), [1986] 1 SCR 190 at 207 for this proposition, where LeDain J stated: “I am of the opinion that the word ‘costs’ must carry the general connotation of being for the purpose of indemnification or compensation.” [35] However, the Supreme Court in Okanagan Indian Band also said that “courts have recognized that indemnity to the successful party is not the sole purpose, and in some cases not even the primary purpose of a costs award” (para 22). When costs awards are employed as instruments of policy, as was the case in Okanagan Indian Band, other considerations may apply. As an instrument of policy, the so-called “modern” approach to costs awards “accomplish[es] various purposes in addition to the traditional objective of indemnification” (para 25). For instance, it may be designed to discourage unnecessary steps in litigation, to sanction bad or frivolous behavior, and to encourage settlement (see paras 22–25). See too 1465778 Ontario Inc v 1122077 Ontario Ltd (2006), 2006 CanLII 35819 (ON CA), 82 OR (3d) 757 at para 26 (CA); and Catalyst Paper Corp v Companhia de Navegação Norsul, 2009 BCCA 16 at para 16. Okanagan Indian Band also discusses the importance of promoting access to justice through costs awards (see paras 23, 26, 27–30). [36] However, where, as in this case, the plaintiff advanced what was found to be a meritorious claim which the defendant defended vigorously, Okanagan Indian Band suggests that indemnification should be the principal consideration. [37] It is accepted that indemnification of the successful party should not normally provide full indemnity for all legal fees and disbursements. Instead, a typical costs award (i.e. party and party costs) is intended to be “a partial indemnity for the expenses to which the recipient has been put as a result of the litigation” (Orkin at 1–3). Cost awards in all Canadian jurisdictions typically constitute only partial indemnification of the litigant's legal costs (Okanagan at para 53). … [41] In Alberta, the weight of authority is that party and party costs should normally represent partial indemnification of the successful party at a level approximating 40–50% of actual costs (see Weatherford CA at para 11; Hill v Hill, 2013 ABCA 313 at para 11; Young v Alberta (Assessors' Association Practice Review Committee/Executive Committee), 2020 ABQB 493 at para 17; Styles v Caravan Trailer Lodges of Alberta Ltd, 2019 ABQB 558 at para 47; Remington v Crystal Creek Homes Inc, 2018 ABQB 644 at para 36; Weatherford QB at para 54; Athabasca Minerals Inc v Syncrude Canada Ltd, 2018 ABQB 551 at para 59; Strategic Acquisition Corp v Multus Investment Corp, 2017 ABQB 297 at para 18; rev'd in part on other grounds 2018 ABCA 63; Blaze Energy Ltd v Imperial Oil Resources, 2014 ABQB 509 at para 68; Calgary (City) v Alberta (Minister of Municipal Affairs), 2008 ABQB 433 at para 42; Marathon Canada Ltd v Enron Canada Corp, 2008 ABQB 770 at para 30; LSI Logic Corp of Canada, Inc v Logani, 2001 ABQB 968 at para 8; Trizec Equities Ltd v Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd, 1999 ABQB 801 at para 20–21, aff'd as to liability only in 1999 ABCA 306). [46] If the option of awarding costs as a percentage of assessed costs is chosen, the assessment of the costs may require a consideration of what is a reasonable amount which ought to have been charged for the services the successful party's lawyer rendered and that may require reference to the considerations set forth in Rule 10.2(1) which go into the determination of what constitutes a reasonable charge (the Rule is reproduced at paragraph 47 herein). If a trial judge chooses to award a percentage of the assessed costs pursuant to Rule 10.31(3)(d) to the successful party, then what is being considered are the “reasonable and proper costs that a party incurred” under Rule 10.31(1)(a). In order to determine whether the costs incurred are reasonable and proper, they must be assessed, either by the party opposite, or by the judge or by an assessment officer. If it is the trial judge, then he or she should consider the reasonableness of both the legal services performed and the amounts charged for those services. Reasonable costs reasonably incurred is what the percentage must be based on. The incurring of the cost must be reasonable and the amount of the cost incurred must also be reasonable. As indicated above, the assessment may also be undertaken by the party opposite or, if the parties cannot reach an agreement on costs, the trial judge may direct an assessment of the legal costs by an assessment officer, pursuant to Rule 10.34. Rule 10.31(3)(d) contemplates such an assessment when it speaks of one party being ordered to pay the other “a percentage of assessed costs” (emphasis added). [47] Among other considerations, an assessment of the reasonableness of the legal costs incurred must take into account the factors set forth in Rule 10.2(1) regarding whether or not a lawyer's fees are reasonable as between the lawyer and his or her client …. [48] That the lawyer's charges are reasonable as between solicitor and client is not the end of the assessment. Consideration must also be given in assessing the reasonableness of requiring the unsuccessful party to indemnify the successful party for a percentage of them. [49] Resorting to Schedule C simply to avoid these assessments may not be appropriate if Schedule C does not yield an appropriate level or scale of indemnification; that is, a reasonable or meaningful level of indemnification. … [51] As a general principle, we see no reason to depart from the 40–50% level of indemnification approved by this Court in Weatherford CA and Hill v Hill. It provides a reasonable guideline upon which the level of indemnification implied by the phrase “reasonable and proper costs” may be measured under the Rules. However, we refrain from defining with any precision the level of indemnification required in any given case. All we say is that the level of indemnification must be both meaningful and reasonable. The court's discretion to move up or down from that level having regard to the factors set forth in Rule 10.33 or in Rule 10.2(1) remains intact. Also, the level of indemnification may be higher or lower than the 40–50% depending on how the litigation was conducted and other factors not necessarily having anything to do with the conduct of the litigation. … [53] As discussed earlier, Schedule C provides little guidance as to what constitutes an appropriate level of indemnification. Rather, it is one of a number of tools that a trial judge may use in order to make a cost award which provides appropriate indemnification. The Rules make it clear that Schedule C may not always constitute “reasonable and proper costs” under Rule 10.31. Indeed, Rule 10.31(3)(a) expressly states that the court may order one party to pay another all or part of its reasonable and proper costs (i.e. the Rule 10.31(1)(a) costs) without reference to Schedule C. Application of Schedule C may yield reasonable and proper costs. It may not. As the majority in Boyd v JBS Foods Canada Inc, 2015 ABCA 191 stated at paragraph 4: “Schedule C is not a standard or starting point. A judge or master need not use it at all”; or as was noted by this Court in Hill: “[w]e must keep in mind that Schedule C is a purely-optional rubber stamp for a judge, who may use it or not, or amend it as he or she sees fit” (para 38). … [58] That said, we should not be taken as questioning the utility of Schedule C, which is provided for in the Rules of Court and which is used day in and day out by judges in a great variety of situations. [59] Schedule C is expressly available under Rules 10.31(3)(a) and (b) as a mechanism or method by which a reasonable and proper costs award may be arrived at (i.e. a costs award pursuant to Schedule C or “a multiple, proportion or fraction of an amount set out in any column … of Schedule C). The Schedule provides a convenient and transparent foundation for judicial determination of costs (GO Community Centre at para 89) and may be appropriate in the “common stream of litigation” (Trizec Equities at para 27) and particularly useful and efficient in high-volume interlocutory matters such as chambers applications (see GO Community Centre at para 89). Schedule C assists judges in making expeditious costs decisions (Rules Project 2005) and may, with or without the use of multipliers, provide a reasonable level of indemnity when such indemnity is called for. [60] Schedule C can also be a useful default to which parties may defer, or which trial judges may adopt in a variety of circumstances. For example, in cases in which there is a significant imbalance in the power and means of the parties, Schedule C, notwithstanding its limitations vis-à-vis indemnity, may be preferable (Styles at para 59). See too Blaze Energy at para 75, Monco Holdings Ltd v BAT Development Ltd, 2005 ABQB 851 at para 31, and Geophysical Service Incorporated v Falkland Oil and Gas Limited, 2019 ABQB 314 at para 23, which express concerns over a percentage-based indemnity approach to costs awards because such an approach may impede access to justice. These concerns may and should be addressed by trial judges on a case-by-case basis, where a Schedule C approach to costs may provide a more equitable result. [61] Finally, we note that Schedule C may be useful simply as a tool of reference for trial judges to make a “reality check” when fashioning an appropriate costs award (see Athabasca at para 61). [62] At the end of the day, the real question faced by trial judges is how to achieve a reasonable and proper costs award, not the steps taken to achieve that result (see Caterpillar Tractor Co at para 4 and Bell Mobility Inc v Anderson, 2015 NWTCA 3 at para 99). Schedule C, while not properly considered a guideline or standard when assessing what constitutes an appropriate level of indemnification, is nevertheless a valuable tool that may effectively be used by trial judges in a variety of situations to make a reasonable and proper costs award. In Weatherford Canada Partnership v. Addie, 2018 ABQB 571, 2018 CarswellAlta 1501, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 248, 26 C.P.C. (8th) 311, Justice Shelley gave a summary of the options available to a Court when granting costs. At paragraphs 23-46, Justice Shelley stated that costs awards depend on the complexity and duration of the litigation, party misconduct, and the remedy sought in the litigation. At paragraphs 47-49, Justice Shelley set out that Courts may apportion costs based on party involvement. Justice Shelley further noted at paragraphs 50-53 that Courts may allow disbursements for legal counsel from other jurisdictions, and, at paragraphs 54-57, her Ladyship provided her conclusion regarding the common approach. For an example of a Court applying the “percentage of the winning party's actual costs” (see paragraph 54 of Justice Shelley's decision), see: Remington v. Crystal Creek Homes Inc., 2018 ABQB 644, 2018 CarswellAlta 1847, 78 Alta. L.R. (6th) 419, 26 C.P.C. (8th) 264. (6th) 33). In the appeal decision, the Court of Appeal said: [11] The discretion to award costs must be exercised judicially and in line with the factors in r 10.33: Stewart Estate v TAQA North Limited, 2016 ABCA 144 (CanLII) at para 26, 35 Alta LR (6th). The general rule is that costs are awarded on a party and party basis, and that this should represent partial indemnification of the successful party—approximately 40–50% of actual costs: Trizec Equities Ltd v Ellis-Don Management Services Ltd, 1999 ABQB 801 (CanLII) at para 20–21, 251 AR 101; Blaze Energy Ltd v Imperial Oil Resources, 2014 ABQB 509 (CanLII) at para 68, [2014] AJ No 916 (QL). [12] Party and party costs balance two competing interests: the unfairness of requiring a successful party whose conduct is not blameworthy to bear any costs and the chilling effect on parties bringing or defending claims if the unsuccessful party is required to bear all the costs: LSI Logic Corporation of Canada, Inc v Logani, 2001 ABQB 968 (CanLII) at para 5, [2002] 4 WWR 531 (LSI Logic). The result of this balance is the concept of partial indemnification through party and party costs to the successful party. [13] While costs are always in the discretion of the court, the cases recognize that when the litigation is complex and the amount at stake in the action in dispute greatly exceeds column 5, courts may award a multiplier of column 5 to help achieve the level of indemnification appropriate for party and party costs: Rocky Mountain House at para 13. To do so is not an error in principle. [14] An award of solicitor and client costs will be rare and must be based on a finding of intentional misconduct during the litigation. LSI Logic at paras 5–6; Luft v Taylor, Zinkhofer & Conway, 2017 ABCA 228 (CanLII) at para 75, 53 Alta LR (6d) 44 (Luft). Solicitor and client costs indemnify for costs that arise within the four corners of the litigation. Full indemnification costs, also known as solicitor and own client costs, compensate for services that are not strictly essential to the litigation. LSI Logic at para 4; Luft at para 77. They are “virtually unheard of” except when provided for by contract: Luft at para 78. In relation to the “percentage indemnity approach” to costs, Justice Renke, in GO Community Centre v. Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd, 2020 ABQB 203, 2020 CarswellAlta 548, said: [163] In my opinion, the percentage indemnity approach, despite the concerns raised, remains a viable approach to costs assessment outside of its traditional application in lengthy, complex proceedings. The availability of this approach, however, is best confined to narrow circumstances such as litigation with substantial sums at stake, involving significant legal or factual complexities, between sophisticated parties on an equal economic footing. In Ford v. New Democrats of Canada Association, 2024 ABCA 395, the Court of Appeal reaffirmed that their decision in McAllister v. Calgary (City), supra, does not reduce the calculation of costs to a simple exercise, without more, of applying a percentage figure to a lawyer's bill. The Court said: [21] The chambers judge was correct that the Master overread the decision in McAllister. While a judge has a considerable discretion in awarding costs, it was not contemplated that the judge would simply award a percentage of solicitor and client costs without undertaking any other analysis. For one thing, this overlooks the primary importance of ensuring that costs incurred are proportionate to the issues. As noted in V.L.M. v Dominey Estate, 2023 ABCA 382, 65 Alta LR (7th) 281: 8 With respect to any costs award, particularly one based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees, the issue is not what counsel actually charged the successful litigant, but what costs should have been incurred in the litigation having regard to all of the relevant circumstances. The issue is not whether the fee charged to the client is fair to the client, but what amount the unsuccessful party can fairly be expected to contribute: Barkwell (#1) at paras. 57-59; Barkwell v McDonald (#2), 2023 ABCA 183 at paras. 74-75; Kantor v Kantor, 2023 ABCA 329 at paras. 12-13. 9 The overriding issue is proportionality. The rules on costs aim to balance indemnity of the winner without unreasonably discouraging access to the court, or unduly penalizing the losing party: McAllister at para. 45; Barkwell (#1) at para. 57. One of the dangers of a costs award based on a percentage of solicitor and client fees is that there is no clear disincentive to overly zealous, inefficient, or disproportionate litigation. In short, success is not a justification for disproportionate litigation. In these circumstances the review of the accounts is not to determine if the amount charged to the client was reasonable and consistent with the retainer, but rather what proportion of those amounts it is fair to expect that the unsuccessful party will pay. While determining if the firm “padded its time” or “ran up unnecessary time on the file” would be relevant (although not determinative) in a review of a solicitor and client account, the proportionality analysis on an assessment of party and party costs goes well beyond that. An assessment officer will rarely be in a position to assess the appropriateness of a cost award without detailed guidance from the judge who made the award. [22] Schedule C has as its basis an assumption about the relationship between the costs it would generate and proportionate solicitor and client costs that should have been incurred for similar pieces of litigation. Where a trial judge does not believe it is appropriate to engage in a detailed analysis of the actual legal expenses of the parties, the default procedure should be to use Schedule C, not to make a blanket award of a percentage of solicitor client costs. The power was inherent in the Court of Chancery and has survived today: Perry v. Perry, [1917] 3 W.W.R. 315; affirmed [1918] 2 W.W.R. 485 (Man. C.A.). It is also contemplated by the Rules of Court: 600. (1) … (a) “costs” includes all the reasonable and proper expenses which any party has paid or become liable to pay for the purpose of carrying on or appearing as a party to any proceeding, including, without restricting the generality of the foregoing … (emphasis added) The traditional test is who is the real promoter of the litigation? Once that is determined exposure to liability for costs may arise should that litigation fail: Orkin, The Law of Costs (1968), citing Curry v. Davison (1922), 23 O.W.N. 3, and Marchiori v. Fewster, (sub nom. St. Lawrence Underwriters' Agency of Western Assurance Co. v. This is the argument that the Society was an unnamed party to the litigation and, as such, should properly bear its portion of the costs. I would not discount the possibility that a court might properly hold an unnamed party liable for costs. The rule is that a non-party who has put forward another person in whose name the proceedings are taken cannot escape liability for costs in putting forward another: R. v. Sturmer and Town of Beaverton[(1912), 25 O.L.R. 566 (Div. Ct.)]. The court's ability to award costs against non-parties was also considered in Jones v. Green (1995), 35 Alta. L.R. (3d) 136 (Q.B.), by Mr. Justice Lutz. In Jones, an action arising out of a motor vehicle accident, two insurance companies (Canada West and Oxford) which had issued underinsured motorist endorsements had successfully applied to become defendants. By the terms of the order, they were given leave to “take issue with the plaintiff with respect to all matters arising in the pleadings, including but not limited to liability, quantum, and costs.” At the conclusion of the trial, Canada West and Oxford took the position that they should not be subject to costs. At pp. 141–43, Lutz J. said: In the normal course of things, costs follow the event. The Defendants by Order do not dispute this principle, but say that they are not “parties” in the true sense, but are more like “intervenors”. They argue that costs should be awarded against the defendants Green and Klopp only… The first objection that Canada West and Oxford raise to an award of costs against them is that costs are a matter to be determined between parties. Canada West and Oxford maintain that they are not parties, but are merely interested persons looking out for their legitimate financial interests. As judgment has been sought and rendered only against Green and Klopp, it is argued that costs should only be awarded against those defendants. Canada West and Oxford take the position that they are in the same position as an insurer defending an action in the name of its insured. An insurer is neither directly liable for costs of an action defended on behalf of the insured, nor is it entitled to costs if it successfully defends such an action: Orkin, The Law of Costs (2nd ed.) (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 1994), § 209.8. I am urged to extend this principle and apply it to the situation of an underinsurer acting against its own insured. It is not the law that costs can only be awarded between a plaintiff and defendant. The authority to award costs is found in s. 19 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. C-29: 19. Subject to an express provision to the contrary in any enactment, the costs of and incidental to any matter authorized to be taken before the Court or a judge are in the discretion of the Court or judge and the Court or judge may make any order relating to costs that is appropriate in the circumstances. Nowhere is this jurisdiction circumscribed so as to allow only for an award of costs against a plaintiff or defendant. It is the presence of an individual before the Court that gives the Court the authority to award costs, and that authority is not dependent on an individual's status as plaintiff or defendant. Div.), where it was said that: It is clear, the underinsurer has a fundamental right to litigate. With that right the underinsurer assumes the responsibility and risks of the litigation. In awarding costs against the third party, Wilson J. said the following (at p. 375): It is my view, therefore, that when the third party is given all the rights of defending an action to the same extent as if a defendant in the action, it must take all of the responsibilities that go with an unsuccessful defence of an action as between it and the plaintiff relating to costs which it caused the plaintiff to incur. I make no comment whatsoever concerning the rights and liabilities between the plaintiff Henriksson and the third party. When the insurer was joined as a third party, the plaintiff served it with notice to produce documents. The insurer refused to produce, arguing that its rights and obligations were set out completely in s. 306 of the Act, and that the Rules of Court did not apply. Laycraft J.A. (as he then was) delivered the judgment of the Court. He said, at pp. 254–55: When an insurer is given the right to file pleadings to contest the defendant's liability to the plaintiff ‘to the same extent as if it were a defendant in the action’, the Rules of Court, of necessity, must govern the rights and obligations of the parties. The right to discovery on the issues raised, including the production of documents is another incident of being a defendant. To free an insurer of the burdens of the position he is entitled to take as a defendant would be to give it far greater rights than ‘as if it were a defendant’. And later said: In my view an insurer who is added as a defendant under section 306 of the Alberta Insurance Act is in precisely the same position as to either advantages gained from or burdens imposed by the Rules of Court as [is] any other defendant. The principle that can be drawn from this case and the others is that while interested parties such as Oxford and Canada West whose rights and obligations may be affected by the outcome of an action have every right to participate in that action, the right to such participation carries with it certain responsibilities. One of those responsibilities, or as Laycraft J.A. called them “incidents of pleading”, is the payment of costs incurred by the successful party as a result of the intervening party's conduct. As L.R. Morin J. noted in Riddoch v. His Lordship then said (at p. 147): I wish to make it clear that this is not a situation where costs have been awarded against the defendant and then, in a separate action, the plaintiff seeks to recover costs from her underinsurer; that is the very circumstance prohibited by cl. 5(e) of the S.E.F. 44. Here the Plaintiff is seeking to recover costs against her underinsurer not as underinsurer and not pursuant to her insurance policy, but as simply as an unsuccessful opposing party in the tort action. Lutz J. concluded by commenting on the proportion of costs for which the insurers were liable. At pp. 149–50 his Lordship said: I agree that Canada West and Oxford should not be responsible for any costs related to the tort action which were incurred prior to October 17, 1991, the day that they were joined as defendants by order. It is also true that there would have to have had to be a trial in any event in order for the Plaintiff to prove the amount by which her damages exceeded $200,000 so that she could ultimately claim from Canada West under the S.E.F. 44 endorsement. In my view, a careful reading of Witts v. Sax and the other authorities referred to above leads to the conclusion that while the defendants by order must accept responsibility for their actions by assuming the burden of costs, that burden should not relate to the costs of the entire trial but should only relate to the degree to which their participation lengthened the trial. The concern for individual accountability that is so evident in Riddoch, supra, can lead to no other result. That said, the trial that would have taken place “in any event” would have been considerably shorter than the 23 days actually taken had Oxford and Canada West not been involved. As the action was undefended, the Plaintiff would have simply put in her case and moved for judgment. There would have been no cross examination of the Plaintiff's witnesses, and no defence evidence would have been called. My assessment of the evidence is that it would have taken at most 3 days for the Plaintiff to put her case had Canada West and Oxford not participated in the trial. I therefore fix the share of costs of the defendants Green and Klopp at 13.04% and the share of Canada West and Oxford at 86.96%. I want to make it clear that Canada West and Oxford are in no way being “punished” for pursuing their right to participate in this action. The decision to litigate is always a risk; insurers are perhaps better able to appreciate this than any other litigant. On the one hand, by going to trial a defendant may be able to significantly reduce damages or even avoid liability altogether, but on the other hand an unsuccessful defendant faces not only damages but costs as well. Canada West and Oxford did nothing improper in joining the action, they simply took a risk and lost, and are now being asked to pay the price. As noted disbursements are provided for in R. 600(1)(a), which allows the taxation of “all the reasonable and proper expenses which any party has paid or become liable to pay for the purpose of carrying on or appearing as party to any proceeding”. A disbursement must generally be an amount payable to a third party, must be an expense specifically related to the file in question, and must be something over and above the general overhead expenses of the lawyer. A disbursement is not allowed if it is merely a disguised form of fee for the lawyer, as those are to be taxed in accordance with the Schedule. By convention an exception to this rule has evolved in party and party taxations with respect to photocopies, which do not have all of the characteristics of a disbursement, but which are commonly allowed as such to recognize the costs of paper and the copy fees charged for the use and maintenance of the machine. Facsimile machines are now very common, and almost every law office would have one. The cost of having the machine, and the cost of maintaining the telephone line to which the machine is connected, are generally a part of the overhead of the firm. The time it takes to activate the facsimile machine is little more than the time it takes to dial a telephone call, or to put a letter in an envelope and mail it. The Law Society does not regard facsimile charges as being true disbursements. Expenses of this kind are in fact a fee component and must be charged to the client as fees, although they may be itemized separately under the fees heading on an account. The amount claimed by the Defendant for facsimile charges is not a proper disbursement. It reflects an internal charge made by the firm to its clients as a part of its fee structure. In fact, and unfortunately, there is no way of knowing what part of the $1.6 million in security that was ordered in Attila Dogan was made up of the e-discovery claim. … [13] I conclude then on this application much as before, that there is some authority in Alberta and elsewhere in favour of recoverable third-party disbursements for e-discovery. This decision adds to it. No authority squarely against it was brought to my attention. (The issue of recoverable law firm disbursements for e-discovery, though addressed favourably in Harris v Leikin Group Inc, above, does not arise in this case.)

Charges for experts See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. General Principles The Rules provide that the unsuccessful party will pay the reasonable costs of experts' reports. A first thing to note about these provisions is that they do not interfere with the contractual relationship between experts and the party who hired them. In other words, the party who hires experts must pay the contractual cost of obtaining their opinion, except in the unlikely situation where the arrangement between the party hiring the expert and the expert is that the expert would be paid what the court considered to be a reasonable fee. One result of the distinction that must be made between the relationship between the party who hires the expert and the loser who must pay all or part of an expert report is that the expert is not entitled to be represented on the costs hearing related to the expert's fees since the expert's fees will be paid in their entirety by the party who hired them. A second thing to note about these provisions is that the court may determine that the cost of a given report should not be fully paid by the losing party even though the expert's report was useful in advancing the winning party's position. In other words, while a totally useless report which never should have been commissioned will not be required to be paid for by the party opposite, the fact that the court does not require a party opposite to pay the full cost of an expert's report does not necessarily cast any doubt on the value of that report. A third thing to note about experts' reports is the relationship that they bear to lawyers' fees. A winning party to litigation is not usually repaid all of its lawyer's fees; the losing party will only be required to pay a portion of the winning party's lawyer's fees. The amount of lawyer's fees that the losing party will be required to pay is a standardized amount for standardized services; these standardized fees and services are set out in Schedule C to the Rules of Court. The lawyer hired by the winning party may well charge more than the tariff, or charge for services that are not included in the tariff. The reason that the losing party is not required to pay all of the legal fees incurred by the winning party is for social policy: the cost of access to justice might be too high if all of a lawyer's fees to the winning side had to be paid by the losing side. Similar considerations relating to the cost of access to justice must motivate the assessment of reasonbleness of experts' fees. A fourth thing to note about experts' reports is that such reports are required in much litigation where the tendency of the court would perhaps be to make erroneous findings of fact about liability or loss without the assistance of such reports. The court should assess the reasonableness of obtaining the report not from the perspective of trial but from the perspective of the party at the time the expert report was commissioned. If getting the report was reasonable at the time, then the fact that the report was not useful at trial, or was not relied on at trial, or was not accepted at trial, is presumably not a factor that will determine whether the report should be paid for by the parties opposite. A fifth thing to note about the assessment of the cost of experts' reports is that the court's approach should be generous, reminding itself that litigants must make decisions about the retention of experts well before they have completed all trial preparations. Anderson v. Ball (1997), 214 A.R. 332 (Q.B.), at 333–34, per Veit J. In Seidel v. Kerr (2004), 27 Alta. L.R. (4th) 227 (C.A.), Wittmann J.A. said, at p. 230: … The primary factor in allowing expert witness costs is whether, at the time it was incurred, the expenditure was reasonable: Nova, an Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. (1988), 89 A.R. 363 (Q.B.). 2. Categories of Experts There are two categories of experts: In any event, it is my further view that the subrule provides examples of two separate categories of experts whose charges are included in the term “costs”. The first category relates to charges of experts for attendance to give evidence at the trial. The second category, if the court so directs, relates to the charges of experts for investigations and inquiries or assisting in the conduct of the trial. I arrive at this interpretation on the basis that the words “such persons” as used in the subrule refer back generally to the persons listed, namely, “accountants, engineers, medical practitioners or other experts”. I could see some merit to the argument of the plaintiff that the subrule relates only to experts who attended to give evidence at the trial if the word “who” was used in place of the word “for” where it first appears in the subrule. As the rule stands, however, the argument of the plaintiff cannot prevail. Nova, An Alberta Corp. v. Guelph Engineering Co. (1988), 60 Alta. L.R. (2d) 366 at 375 (Q.B.). In Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd. (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 296 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice McMahon dealt with, inter alia, the matter of private investigators fees as a disbursement. The plaintiff had sued a Calgary television station for defamation. He claimed damages in excess of $15.7 million. The defendant was successful at trial and sought investigator's fees in the amount of $252,751.32. His Lordship awarded a disbursement of approximately $200,000 for investigators' fees. The Court of Appeal [(1997), 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 255 (C.A.); reconsideration refused (1998), 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999), 232 A.R. 189 (C.A.)], allowed an appeal from that award. At p. 270, the Court said: That investigatory fee related in large part to keeping track of witnesses and their changes of address… We must emphasize the definition of “costs” in Rule 600(1)(a), “all the reasonable and proper expenses”. In justifying the disbursement, the witnesses were identified as people who were transient and difficult to locate. In this case, it is unknown how many of these witnesses were transient, unwilling, or failed to notify the respondents of any change of address. A $200,000 award represents a significant sum. While judges must often, for practicable purposes, award disbursements on the basis of counsel's representations, when the award is of this magnitude it should not be awarded without evidence as to its necessity and reasonableness. As with costs generally, a notice to admit facts could have resolved this problem. Had the appellants failed to admit the facts involving these witnesses (which were later proven), the respondents would have been entitled to seek reimbursement for the costs of producing the witnesses, including some reasonable sum for keeping track of their whereabouts where that was required. However, no notice to admit was served. Frequently, keeping a list of the current addresses of witnesses is simply part of the overhead of a law firm and should not be the subject of a separate disbursement. As such, it should be included as part of the party and party costs award. The respondents then unsuccessfully applied for a re-hearing before the Court of Appeal [(1998), 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.)]. In Monashee Petroleums Ltd. v. Pan Cana Resources Ltd. (1988), 85 A.R. 183 (C.A.), Mr. Justice Côté at pp. 192–93, made the following observations about awarding costs in respect of experts retained for, but not called at trial: The plaintiff complains that the defendant's party-and-party costs at trial included a fee for an expert who did not testify. The defendant in his factum says that was less than a quarter of the fees charged by that expert. The defendant's expert was apparently held in readiness to rebut the plaintiff's expert who (in the event) only testified subject to objections by the defendant and the learned trial judge's deferring his ruling on the plaintiff's expert's admissibility until judgment. After lengthy cross-examination of the plaintiff's expert, counsel for the defendant did not call his rebuttal expert, possibly correctly divining that the learned trial judge would exclude the evidence of the plaintiff's expert. It has always been the rule that expenditures for witnesses are based on what seemed reasonable at the time, not on hindsight about witnesses who in the event turned out later to be unnecessary. Cost are for proper expenses, and expenses are incurred by ordinary mortals, not by prophets. The trial judge is in a much better position to assess that sort of a situation than an appellate court, and an award of one quarter is modest enough that I see no reason whatever to interfere with what (by rule 601) is a matter of discretion. In Hetu v. Traff (1999), 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 326 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Johnstone, at pp. 331 and 333, gave the following summary of the law: The law is clear that in determining whether an expert witness fee should be allowed, the test is whether the expenditure was reasonable at the time that it was made … Further, the successful party can receive costs for witnesses that were reasonably retained, regardless of whether or not those witnesses testify at trial. . . . . . … professionals that are not qualified as experts can nonetheless be awarded higher fees than that generally allowed for ordinary witnesses when they testify as to the professional services they rendered. 3. Costs Incurred Prior to Commencement of Action In Kha v. Salhab (2001), 282 A.R. 324 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Kenny concluded that costs for interpretive services incurred prior to the commencement of the action are not recoverable costs. At pp. 325, 327, Her Ladyship said: The issue is whether rule 600 of the Alberta Rules of Court contemplates an award of costs in relation to disbursements for interpretation services incurred prior to, yet necessary for, the commencement of a legal action. As counsel indicated, it was necessary for counsel to obtain all of the particulars and have meetings with the plaintiffs in order to determine the appropriate course of action and whether or not that course of action would include commencing a lawsuit. … From a public policy prospective [sic], it does seem somewhat unjust that minority groups in the position of the plaintiffs are liable to incur added expense in hiring an interpreter in order to access justice in the Province. Nevertheless, this seems to be the case in light of the decision in [Bow Island (Municipal District) v. Wortz, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 153 (Alta. C.A.)]. Unless there is a wording change in rule 600 of the Rules of Court that would encompass expenses such as interpreter costs or a re-examination of the law as it currently stands by the decision of the Court of Appeal of Alberta in Wortz, there appears to be nothing this Court can do to assist. In Millott Estate v. Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 2002 CarswellAlta 1551, 322 A.R. 307, 9 Alta. L.R. (4th) 292, Fraser J. followed Kha v. Salhab (2001), 282 A.R. 324 (Q.B.), and, at p. 329, held that “costs necessarily incurred prior to the commencement of an action in order to determine if a case for liability could be made are not allowable under the Rules of Court.” In Davidson v. Patten (2005), 52 Alta. L.R. (4th) 159 (Q.B.), Mahoney J. took a different view. In that case, the ultimately successful plaintiff obtained, before commencing the litigation, a collision re-construction report. Mahoney J. allowed the claim for the expense of that report. At pp. 167–169, he said: Anderson & Associates Pre-Litigation Reports. Andersen & Associates provided the Plaintiff's counsel with a collision re-construction report before the Statement of Claim was filed. The Defendant argues that the law does not provide for disbursements incurred before the action is commenced. When this issue came before Justice Kenny, in Kha v. Salhab, [2001] A.J. No. 61, 2001 ABQB 44 (Q.B.) she clearly felt bound by the decision of the Alberta Court of Appeal in Bow Island (Municipal District) v. Wortz, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 153, to the effect that disbursements incurred prior to the commencement of the action are not recoverable, even if the expenses were necessary. In Millot Estate v. Reinhard (2002), 322 A.R. 307, 2002 ABQB 998 (Q.B.), Justice Fraser came to the same conclusion. The Plaintiff suggests that Justice Fraser erred because it appears that he felt bound by Justice Kenny's decision, but this is clearly a misreading of what Justice Fraser wrote. Justice Fraser felt bound by the current law, not by Justice Kenny's decision alone, and he clearly cited the Court of Appeal decision in Bow Island, as did Justice Kenny. I agree with the Plaintiff's argument that Bow Island itself is distinguishable, because the pre-action costs in that case were not strictly necessary for the proceeding to commence i.e. the costs involved an audit that uncovered fraud, and the audit would have been done in any event. The doctrine of stare decisis, of adherence to precedent, is a crucial feature of the common law. Respect for precedent gives the common law its stability and predictability. At the same time, the possibility of judges changing legal rules allows the law to evolve, to adjust to new circumstances, and therefore to become more efficient over time, leading toward ever better rules. Precedents must be read in the context of their times, and with due regard for changing social, cultural, and criminal facts. (Harper v. A.-G. Can (#1), [2000] 2 SCR 764, 2000 S.C.C. 57. Bow Island was decided in 1921 and within a fact situation unique to that case. Litigation today is more complex and the rules of procedure more flexible. Rule 600(1)(a) uses the phrase “reasonable and proper expenses … for the purpose of carrying on or appearing as a party to any proceeding.” The choice of words “carrying on” must reasonably include the commencement of the proceeding so that a party can recover the expense of filing an initiating document like a statement of claim. Furthermore, if a person requires the services of an interpreter in order to give instructions to a lawyer to commence the proceedings, then that step fits within the ambit of a reasonable and proper expense. It is incongruent that a disbursement, like the cost for the services of an interpreter, or a collision reconstruction report, reasonably and properly incurred by a party regarding an action which does proceed should not qualify as an expense incurred to carry on the proceedings. Otherwise, parties who intend to commence an action are put in the unwarranted predicament of having to rush off and file a statement of claim before collecting relevant information to properly plead their case or preserve evidence that may disappear or be destroyed. This cannot be what the rule intended. In deciding whether to allow or not allow pre-action costs, the question to ask is whether the costs incurred were reasonable and proper. If they are reasonable and proper, they may be allowed. The test is whether it would be reasonable or proper for a reasonable prudent person, endeavouring to get justice, but endeavouring to get it without any undue expense, to incur the costs in question. A judge or a taxing officer, exercising his or her discretion must consider the circumstances of the particular case existing when the cost was incurred and not in relation to the eventual state of circumstances at the trial. Monashee Petroleum Ltd. V. Pan Cong Resources Ltd. (1988), 85 A.R. 183 (C.A.). The Plaintiff at the time of retaining this expert clearly had a cause of action but did not know whether the Defendants would admit liability. The collision was a serious one where it would be reasonable for a party to determine the technical cause through the advice of a professional. Timelines in conducting the investigation and preserving the evidence was an important factor. The expert, Cliff Anderson, a professional engineer, did testify as to the severity of the collision. This is not a situation where a party, such as an insurer, routinely incurs expenses to investigate a claim in order to determine liability and the amount of the claim. Such expenses I would not allow (see Erco Industries Ltd. v. Allendale Mutual Insurance Co. (1984), 13 D.L.R. (4th) 213). The expense of Anderson and Associates reports is a reasonable and proper expense and is allowed as claimed.

Charges of legal agents See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. Legal Agents' Fees as Disbursements In Hetu v. Traff (1999), 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 326 (Q.B.), the successful plaintiff sought as costs the fees paid to agent solicitors for their efforts to locate an out-of-jurisdiction medical expert. The costs were claimed as a disbursement. Johnstone J. disallowed the claim. At p. 337, her Ladyship said: This agency fee is denied for two reasons. Firstly, if allowed, this would have the demonstrated effect of increasing the total legal fees taxable against the other party above the amount prescribed by the legislature for those fees. Secondly, the professional service for locating and retaining experts is a normal task of counsel to seek such experts from outside its own city or province without utilizing an agent.

Plans, models, copies of documents See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. Photocopying charges … within the limits of a situation involving a few copies, the financial burden of the overhead involved in producing a pleading is taken into account in fixing the fee for the work product … Let me add also that, even in the case of party-and-party costs, when numerous copies are needed it is reasonable to allow photocopying costs. Reese v. Alberta (1993), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 at 54–55 (Q.B.). In Clancy v. Gough, 2011 ABQB 778, 2011 CarswellAlta 2179, 523 A.R. 163, 59 Alta. L.R. (5th) 108, Bensler, J. commented on costs claims for printing and photocopying. At paragraphs 54–59, her Ladyship said: 54 Laser printing and photocopying are interesting categories. Clearly having the ability to print and photocopy is a necessary capability to operate any law office, so the associated costs tend to fall within the characterization of overhead. Moreover, given that many firms do actually produce most documents in-house (often using commercial quality printers and photocopiers) the cost associated with printing and photocopying is not a true disbursement paid to a third party. 55 On the other hand, the practice of law is still incredibly document intensive and paper-based, so in my view it is reasonable to allow some level of recovery for printing and photocopying directly related to a particular file. However, I do so cautiously. It seems the rate that many law offices charge for these services is out of touch with the true internal cost, or the equivalent expense that would otherwise be incurred if these services were delivered by a third party commercial printer. 56 That premise seems to apply in this case where counsel for the Defendants informed the Court that its practice is to bill each black and white printed or copied page at 30 cent(s) each, though no independent evidence was introduced in support. I take judicial notice that the commercial cost to the public for similar services is considerably less. For example, at the various Staples Copy and Print Centres around Calgary the cost of printing and photocopying ranges from 3–10 cent(s) per standard page, depending on the quantity of printing ordered. It is also worthy to note that those rates still result in profit to the commercial printer. 57 I find it unreasonable that the Defendants seek to recover from the Plaintiffs a “disbursement” at least three times higher than if the work had actually been performed by a third party. In the words of Wittmann J.A. (as he then was) “one would expect evidence that money was paid to a third party in order to qualify as a disbursement.” While I am willing to allow some level of printing and photocopying, lacking evidence as to the true cost of these services to the law firm, I am not willing to entertain a submission for an expense so out of alignment with commercial reality. If law firms are actually incurring 30 cent(s) to produce every printed or photocopied page then lawyers should be prepared to submit evidence related thereto when attempting to recover these costs from their clients, or the other party. 58 Using the rate provided by counsel and the aggregate charges for these line items on the Bill of Costs, the number of underlying pages can be mathematically calculated. In this manner I have determined the volume of laser printed and photocopied pages was 7369 and 7002, respectively. However, the cost reproducing drafts, or the cost of copying documents such as pleadings, motions and affidavits compensated under another item in the costs schedule, is not recoverable: Millott Estate v. Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 322 A.R. 307 at paras. 72–74. In oral argument counsel for the Defendants estimated that approximately 10% of the total pages produced was used to create ‘final’ documents. As such, I allow 10% of 7369 for laser printing and 10% of 7002 pages for photocopying. 59 Referring back to the publicly available Staples price list, this quantity of standard printing would cost 6 cent(s) per page. While I don't impose the same efficiencies on a law firm as might be incumbent on a commercial printer, I find 10 cent(s) per page to be reasonable in the circumstances. Reducing the rate for printing and photocopying also finds judicial support both in this Court as well as the Alberta Court of Appeal: Lynch at para. 48, Dechant v. Law Society of Alberta, 2001 ABCA 81, 277 A.R. 333 at para. 30, and Marathon Canada Ltd. at para. 53. 2. Rate for Photocopies Each case is decided individually but it is clear that one should produce evidence of the rate being suggested (either as claimant or payor). In Reese v. Alberta (1993), 5 Alta. L.R. (3d) 40 (Q.B.), at p. 56 McDonald J. said: In the present case, without the benefit of any evidence as to the actual cost of photocopying, I am prepared to recognize a cost of 15 cents a page. Still, there is no hard and fast rule, so evidence is preferable. This is so whether one seeks the disbursement or wishes to pay a lower rate. The Court of Appeal has made reference to the problems associated with a failure to provide evidence of the true cost of the disbursement sought. In Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd. (1997), 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 255 (C.A.); [reconsideration refused [(1998), 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999), 232 A.R. 189 (C.A.)], the court said, at p. 271: Finally, the appellants argued that the photocopy charge of 25 cents per page is not a true disbursement. They argued that the true cost of photocopying should be in the neigbourhood of 3 to 5 cents, and that any amount above this should be included in overhead costs. Unfortunately, there was no evidentiary basis for the argument and accordingly we leave it to another day whether a 25 cent charge for such disbursements is excessive. The trial judge allowed this amount as a disbursement and we do not disturb this portion of the award. In Dechant v. Stevens, 2001 ABCA 81, 2001 CarswellAlta 356, 277 A.R. 333, 89 Alta. L.R. (3d) 289; leave to appeal refused 2001 CarswellAlta 1211, [2001] 3 S.C.R. vi, a rate of $.25 per page was sought for photocopying. The court, per curiam, said: … copying is a legitimate disbursement. If [Dechant] can prove that she has paid 25 cents a page to some arm's length person, the fee should be allowed. Otherwise we order 15 cents a page. Photocopying is a difficult disbursement to address. Evidence in a given case may show that there should be no charge for photocopies for the represented litigant because the cost associated with copying is just part of the overhead of the firm which is compensated by a general costs order. Alternatively, there may be evidence in a given case as to the actual costs incurred as a result of farming out the expense to a third party. It may even be that a general costs award should be higher for the unrepresented litigant who does not receive a costs award over and above disbursements. In Fill v. Somani, 2013 ABQB 572, 2013 CarswellAlta 1858, 571 A.R. 230, Justice Shelley awarded $0.28 per photocopy page, stressing that the evidence before the Court supported the claim. Justice Shelley said, at paragraphs 61 and 63: 61 The Plaintiffs submit that the in-house photocopying costs should be awarded at the rate of $0.28 per page. This position is supported by Affidavit evidence of Jennifer Paolucci, a Legal Assistant employed by Plaintiffs' counsel. Ms. Paolucci's Affidavit details the various costs associated with the photocopying of documents and concludes that the actual costs of photocopying are approximately $0.38 per page. … 63 The Defendants do not provide any evidence which suggests that the analysis undertaken by Ms. Paolucci was erroneous in any way. Where a party does not provide evidence to support a higher amount, Courts have arbitrarily set an amount. However, where there is evidence to support a higher number, Courts have awarded it. Here, Ms. Paolucci's evidence confirms actual photocopying costs of $0.38 per page. I conclude that the requested amount of $0.28 per page has been proven, since there is no evidence or analysis to contradict it. Accordingly, the amount claimed will be awarded. 3. Meaning of “copies of documents” In Millott Estate v. Reinhard, 2002 ABQB 998, 2002 CarswellAlta 1551, 322 A.R. 307, 9 Alta. L.R. (4th) 292, the successful plaintiff sought $14,626.92 in photocopying charges. Fraser J. allowed $2500.00, and discussed the meaning of the phrase “copies of documents” at pp. 326–328: [72] The cost of producing copies of documents required for use in the trial including expert reports, exhibits, and arguments and other documents which must be served, is in my view a cost which can be passed on. However, the cost of repeated photocopying of drafts of documents prepared for use in the action such as arguments, or of other miscellaneous documents such as letters, is not. [73] Rule 600(1)(a)(iv) governs the right to claim the cost of photocopying as a disbursement. … [74] The reference to “copies of documents” in my opinion is to final copies of existing documents such as those listed in paragraph 72 above. It does not cover copies of drafts. Nor does it cover “the preparation of copies of pleadings, notices of motion, affidavits, orders and so on which is covered by Rule 605(3) and cannot be included if the copy in question is a copy of a document used in completing some step already covered by another item included in the Bill of Costs”. Per McDonald, J. (as he then was), in Ukrainian (Edmonton) Credit Union Ltd. v. 258753 Alberta Ltd., Gourdine and Olsen (1984), 60 A.R. 148 (Q.B.).

Other Charges See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.31. 1. Lost Wages In Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd. (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 296 (Q.B.); [varied on other grounds (1997) 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 255 (C.A.); reconsideration refused (1998) 216 A.R. 151 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1999) 232 A.R. 189 (C.A.)], McMahon J. allowed a claim for conduct money to include amounts paid to witnesses as compensation of wages lost due to attendance at trial. Special circumstances would appear to be necessary to warrant such an award. At p. 303, his Lordship said: The defence paid conduct money for their witnesses and, as well, paid travel accommodation and meal expenses where incurred. In a few cases they appear to have paid a day's wages lost for attendance at trial. Given the number of witnesses and the obvious scheduling difficulties in a lengthy trial of this kind, these disbursements do not seem inordinate. I specifically allow the payment for lost wages where paid instead of the daily witness fee provided by Sched. C. I do so because of my findings as detailed in the Reasons for Judgment that the tenants and former tenants (who comprised most of the witnesses) had been poorly treated by the plaintiffs. They have suffered enough loss without having to incur further loss as a consequence of giving testimony. 2. Conduct Money For One's Own Officers and Employees In Parrish & Heimbecker Ltd. v. All Peace Auctions Ltd. (2002), 326 A.R. 383, a defendant was successful at trial. The defendant sought as part of its costs conduct money for its employees and officers who attended examinations for discovery and trial. An informal agreement had been reached by counsel to produce officers and employees at discoveries without the need of formal appointments and without payment of conduct money. At p. 389, Phillips J. said: W.A. Stevenson and J.E. Côté, Civil Procedure Guide, vol. 2 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 1996) states, at 1938, that parties are entitled to conduct money as part of a costs award regardless of whether a demand for conduct money was made. Further, an agreement between counsel to forego formal appointments and the payment of conduct money at the time, does not prevent a party from seeking costs in this regard. Accordingly, I find that All Peace is entitled to conduct money for the attendance of its employees and officers at trial and examinations for discovery for those days when evidence was being given by these individuals. 3. Lump Sum Costs In Wener v. Wener, an unreported decision of the Alberta Court of Appeal rendered June 8, 1971, Calgary Appeal Number 7912, the court concluded that the discretion to award a lump sum in lieu of taxing costs can be exercised only where the trial judge has full information about the work done and the disbursements incurred. If true for taxable costs, it must also be true for solicitor/client costs. Markdale Ltd. v. Ducharme (1998), 238 A.R. 98 (Q.B.), at 106, per Bielby J. [leave to appeal refused (1998), 238 A.R. 321 (Q.B.)].
